hard_gates.gate: G1 tenant isolation: my own live attack as tenant A (alnoor) on tenant B (gulfsteel), API, exports, jobs, files
hard_gates.evidence:
I reused the r20 critic script (attack/attack.mjs). It ran 246 operations with B's ids, 1,656 documented query-parameter requests, 1,065 tenant-switch requests (headers, query, cookies), 190 export requests, 77 filter requests and 331 path-variant and audit requests. B's rows in all 29 tenant tables were the same before the attack, after it, and again after A's queued cleanup job had run (attack/b-before-attack.txt = b-after-attack.txt = b-now.txt). I explained all 137 flagged lines (attack/probe.txt):
- 81 audit-record reads with B ids gave answers identical to a random id (54/54 in the probe).
- 'Gulf Steel' and 'الخليج' are in A's own data (143 and 1,633 alnoor contacts).
- B's tenant id in A's audit log is A's own attack job payload ({"tenantId": B} on A's jobs.cleanup, which ran in alnoor only).
- DELETE of B's rate or file answered 204, but so does a random id, and B still reads both while A gets 404.
A's list totals did not move when B wrote.

hard_gates.gate: G1 tenant isolation: the database role the app uses
hard_gates.evidence:
The app connects only as erp_app and the worker as erp_app plus erp_worker. No erp role is superuser or has BYPASSRLS (db-roles.txt). Every one of the 29 tenant tables has RLS enabled and forced and a NOT NULL tenant_id, and none is owned by erp_app. erp_app can read no table without tenant_id. As erp_app (db-app-role-attack.txt):
- Nothing is visible with no tenant set, with a session-level app.tenant_id, or with a session-level tenant_tx marker.
- SET ROLE erp_owner/erp_worker/erp_auth is refused, and so is row_security=off.
- ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE RLS is refused, as are pg_stat_user_tables, pg_class, pg_read_file and lo_import.
- The value functions, including this round's new customfields.value_date_trunc, return nothing for a B record unbound or bound to A, and the value when bound to B.

biggest_gap.title: A full verify still takes about 2 h 50 min on the shared machine, and its counted processor time (24,705 s) is already above the maximum the round was built against
biggest_gap.detail:
Every gate held, every test passed in run 2, and the r20 partition-check fault is fixed. What most holds the foundation back now is the cost of proving it, the same as in r19:
- Run 2 took 10,025 s of wall time before its ratchet step (run 1 took 10,805 s). The ratchet's own target for a quiet machine is 3,600 s.
- The four G1 HTTP attack shares took about 48 min to 1 h 22 min each, at 2,650 to 3,560 processor seconds per share.
- The dotnet stage alone counted 21,218 s, and the whole verify 24,705 s, against the 23,300 s maximum of this commit. The maximum was since raised to 24,500 at d71aae0c, so even that is exceeded on a busy machine.
- The ratchet saw 78.9 % of the machine's processor time as 'other work' (116,860 s on the machine, 24,705 s counted), so the counted number still understates the real cost of the test databases and stacks.
Every new endpoint makes each critic and integrator round longer and pushes the next piece's first integration over the maximum again. Builders need a cheaper per-endpoint HTTP attack, or a cost line that counts what the tests really use.
biggest_gap.evidence:
verify-critic-p00-foundation-r21-run2.log, ratchet lines:
- 'verify wall time before the ratchet: 10025 s (maximum on a quiet machine 3600 s; not judged: the machine was busy (load 7.34 at the start, 3.31 at the end, highest 66.74 ...'
- 'verify processor time: 24705 s (dotnet 21218, web 2658, e2e 740, timing 90; maximum 23300 s)'
- 'machine processor time over the run: 116860 s; verify stages 24705 s; other work beside the verify 92155 s (78.9 % ...)'
